The Next AI Infrastructure Race: Technology Is Not Enough — Ecosystem Leadership Matters

Elon Musk’s public expression of interest in hiring Jensen Huang has sparked an interesting conversation across the technology industry.

But beyond the headlines, I believe there is a much bigger question worth exploring:

What makes a leader truly valuable in the AI infrastructure era?

Jensen Huang’s contribution to NVIDIA goes far beyond GPU innovation.

Over the past three decades, NVIDIA has built an ecosystem connecting semiconductor technology, computing architecture, networking, software developers, server manufacturers, cloud providers and enterprise customers.

This is not simply a technology business. It is an integrated industrial ecosystem.

And this is where the significance of Musk’s interest becomes particularly interesting.

As AI infrastructure continues to scale, competitive advantages will increasingly depend on more than access to advanced chips or computing capacity.

They will depend on the ability to connect multiple critical resources:

• Technology: GPUs, AI servers, networking and computing platforms.

• Energy: Reliable power supply, energy storage and efficiency.

• Infrastructure: Data centers, land, cooling and connectivity.

• Capital: Long-term investment and financing capabilities.

• Ecosystem: Strategic partnerships, supply chains, enterprise customers and execution capabilities.

These elements do not operate independently. Their value comes from how effectively they are integrated.

For Southeast Asia, this presents both an opportunity and a challenge.

Markets such as Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia are increasingly important in the regional AI infrastructure landscape. However, sustainable growth will require more than building data center capacity.

It will require stronger coordination between investors, infrastructure developers, technology providers, energy partners and enterprise customers.

My takeaway:

The next phase of AI infrastructure competition may not be won by those who simply own the most advanced technology or the largest computing capacity.

It may be shaped by those who can bring the right resources, partners and capabilities together — and turn them into commercially viable, scalable ecosystems.

In the AI era, ecosystem leadership could become one of the most important competitive advantages.

The world is paying closer attention to one leadership question:
Are we selecting the right leader, for the right position, at the right time?
This principle applies to corporations, governments, professional associations, non-profit organizations, and institutions of every kind.

I have been hiring people since 1994, many of whom are now Board members of Indonesia’s leading companies. Since 2020, I have also served as an assessor for candidates for Director positions in large institutions. One lesson has remained consistent: leadership requirements change as organizations evolve.

A business in crisis may need a decisive turnaround leader. A growing company may need someone who can build systems, strengthen execution, and develop people. A mature institution may need a leader who can renew its culture while protecting its core strengths.
A leader who succeeded in one situation may not be the right leader for another.

Whether an organization thrives or declines depends partly on whom we select, how we select them, and why we choose them.

The consequences of poor appointments can be significant:
- Strategy may not translate into execution.
- Culture may deteriorate.
- Capable people may disengage or leave.
- Governance risks may increase.
- Stakeholder confidence may decline.
- Growth opportunities may be missed.

Why do organizations sometimes appoint the wrong person?
Personal loyalty, fear of capable challengers, the desire for control, favouritism, nepotism, political considerations, personal interests, pride, and simple convenience can all influence judgment.

These motives are human. Most leaders do not intend to harm their organization. However, good intentions must be supported by clear criteria, independent assessment, transparent governance, and regular review.

Gallup has observed that “deciding who should be named manager has a ripple effect on everything else.”

For C-level leaders and Boards, the questions are worth asking:
- Is this person suitable for the organization’s current stage?
- Do they have the character, judgment, capability, and capacity required?
- Can they build trust, make difficult decisions, develop people, and serve the organization’s long-term interests?
- Are we selecting this person for performance and potential, or because they are familiar and loyal?

The right appointment is a business decision, a governance decision, and a stewardship decision.

The right leader, in the right place, at the right time can strengthen performance, culture, resilience, and stakeholder trust.

But for me, participating in a hiring event is never just about recruitment numbers: how many people register, how many CVs we collect, or how many candidates we can bring into the pipeline.

I see it as something much bigger.
While people may already know Haloka as a Brand Thinking Partner through its work with clients, I believe there's another side of the brand worth introducing:Haloka as a place to grow, contribute, and build meaningful things together.

Through initiatives like this, I want more people to get to know Haloka Group Indonesia, understand what we do, discover the people behind the brand, and hopefully see themselves as part of the team someday.

Beyond employer branding, I also see this as an opportunity to build relationships, expand our network, exchange perspectives, and open doors to collaborations and opportunities that may come from unexpected connections, not necessarily limited to business or client relationships.

And honestly, that's what makes experiences like this so exciting for me as an HR professional. It's not just about finding the right people for the company, but also making the company more visible and approachable to the right people.

B50 Biodiesel: What Changes When Half Your Diesel Comes From Palm Oil

A light technical read for fleet operators, engineers and the simply curious

Indonesia keeps nudging the biodiesel dial higher. B30 became B35, B40 became the national standard in 2025, and now B50 means half the diesel in your tank is no longer fossil fuel. For anyone running trucks, generators or heavy equipment, the practical question is simple: what does that do to an engine?

What B50 actually is

B50 is a blend of 50 percent fatty acid methyl ester (FAME) biodiesel and 50 percent petroleum diesel, by volume. In Indonesia the FAME comes from refined palm oil, converted through transesterification, where triglycerides react with methanol to form methyl esters and glycerol.

Why a country goes this far

Indonesia is the world's largest palm oil producer and still a net importer of diesel, so every liter of domestic biodiesel is a liter that doesn't need importing. Government estimates put the foreign-exchange savings well above a hundred trillion rupiah, though they swing with crude and palm oil prices. Critics fairly add that the emissions benefit depends on how the palm was grown.

What it does inside the engine

Palm-based biodiesel has a high cetane number and good lubricity, which helps ignition and protects pumps and injectors. The trade-off is energy content. Pure FAME holds about 8 percent less energy per liter, so at B50 expect consumption to rise by a few percent at most.

FAME is also a mild solvent that loosens old deposits, so fleets often change filters more often in the first few weeks. It absorbs water more readily than diesel and oxidizes faster, so keep tanks dry and don't store fuel for months. Cold flow is rarely a concern in the tropics.

A few habits make life easier: drain water from separators regularly, keep spare fuel filters on hand during the first month after switching, and rotate stock instead of letting fuel sit.

Most modern diesel engines are expected to cope with B50, but check the manufacturer's guidance first. Older rubber seals can degrade, and engines with particulate filters may need shorter oil change intervals.

Choosing a B50 supplier

Blend quality matters as much as the ratio. Ask where the FAME comes from, how consistent each batch is, and whether a certificate of analysis (against SNI 7182) comes with every delivery. A low B50 biodiesel price can hide off-spec fuel that costs far more in filters and downtime. A reliable B50 fuel supplier should also handle bulk B50 biodiesel delivery to mines, plantations, ports and industrial sites on schedule. One standard answer rarely fits a plantation, a mining contractor and a logistics fleet, so it helps to work with a distributor that understands your operation.

THE CARGO THAT EATS THE SHIP
5 mm-deep pitting in just 50 days. When sulphur meets moisture, hidden damage can begin beneath the cargo.

A bulk carrier can transport thousands of tonnes of sulphur. But what happens when the cargo threatens the very steel structure carrying it?

According to Brookes Bell’s technical investigation (19 August 2026), inspections documented:

* Localised pitting reaching 5 mm in unprotected steel in approximately 50 days.
* Steel wastage of up to 7 mm in some cases.
* Limewash coating protection lasting approximately 30 days.

The report cites a seawater corrosion rate of approximately 0.2 mm/year. On a simple annualised mathematical comparison, the reported pitting rate is approximately 182 times the cited seawater corrosion rate. This is an indicative comparison, not a prediction of uniform steel loss across the vessel.

Source: Brookes Bell – Sulphur Cargo Damage
https://lnkd.in/eaySVUQE

What causes the damage?

Dry sulphur does not normally react aggressively with bare steel. The risk increases when moisture, sulphur and exposed steel interact, creating conditions for acidic and electrochemical corrosion.

Limewash acts as a protective and neutralising barrier. However, once it deteriorates, the underlying steel becomes vulnerable.

Source: UK P&I Club – Carefully to Carry, Sulphur Cargoes
https://lnkd.in/eNCJ3wN6

The risk is real. DNV documented a historical bulk carrier case involving groove corrosion reaching 9 mm in depth following sulphur carriage.

Source: DNV – Corrosive Cargo in Holds
https://lnkd.in/eDyUEfDv

The commercial impact

Dark sulphur scale can make a cargo hold appear more damaged than the actual steel loss. Ultrasonic thickness measurements and professional marine inspections are therefore essential.

Brookes Bell estimates that wholesale steel renewal can cost approximately 10 times more than targeted localised repairs.

The consequences include vessel downtime, repair and chartering costs, insurance exposure, discharge delays and reduced transaction profitability.

A question for the global sulphur trade:

Are we assessing only the cargo’s quality, quantity and price — or also the condition and suitability of the vessel carrying it?

In commodity trading, securing the cargo is only part of the equation. The condition of the vessel carrying it matters just as much.
